prompt: What happens in a debrief where the first speaker says “strong hire” before anybody has written anything?

choices.text: The others argue harder against it
choices.why: The research on anchoring finds the opposite tendency.

choices.text: They drift towards it
choices.why: Right: four interviews become one opinion held four times.

choices.text: Nothing, if the interviewers are experienced and have run many debriefs together before
choices.why: Experience does not remove anchoring; process does.

choices.text: The decision is delayed
choices.why: Usually it is reached faster, which is part of the problem.

prompt: Why does Renata, the hiring manager, speak last in the debrief?

choices.text: Hers is the opinion most likely to anchor the room
choices.why: Right: she makes the decision, so hearing her first would pull everybody towards it.

choices.text: Out of politeness
choices.why: The reason is structural, not manners.

choices.text: Because Caju’s hiring tool only reveals her feedback once everybody else has spoken aloud
choices.why: The tool hides feedback until each person submits; speaking order is Renata’s own rule.

choices.text: She has the least evidence
choices.why: She interviewed too; the issue is her power over the decision.

prompt: Why may nobody change their written score during the debrief?

choices.text: The original records what each of them thought before hearing anybody, which calibration needs
choices.why: Right: scores written after a discussion measure the discussion.

choices.text: Changing your mind is not allowed
choices.why: They can say they now see it differently, and it goes in the notes.

choices.text: The tool locks the score
choices.why: The rule is Renata’s, for a reason.

choices.text: To stop the debrief from running over the thirty minutes the calendar invitation allowed
choices.why: Time is not the reason.

prompt: Match each bias with what it does in an interview.

pairs.right: one strong impression spreads to everything else
people who resemble the interviewer are rated higher
evidence for a first impression is sought, and evidence against discounted
a candidate looks stronger after a weak one

prompt: In Bertrand and Mullainathan’s 2004 study, what differed between the CVs?

choices.text: The university attended
choices.why: Everything but the name was the same.

choices.text: The years of experience listed on each one, which varied from one to ten years
choices.why: Experience was held constant.

choices.text: The photograph
choices.why: There were no photographs; the name was the only difference.

choices.text: Only the name
choices.why: Right: names perceived as white got about 50% more callbacks for the same CV.

prompt: Why does the lesson say resolving to be more careful does little against bias?

choices.text: Interviewers do not care about fairness
choices.why: The lesson assumes good intentions and explains why they are not enough.

choices.text: They are not choices
choices.why: Right: nobody sees their own halo from inside it; changing the conditions works better.

choices.text: Because bias is rare among experienced interviewers, so there is little left for care to fix
choices.why: The research is mostly on people who believed they were fair.

choices.text: Care takes too long
choices.why: Time is not the argument.

prompt: Which of the lesson’s countermeasures targets the halo effect?
hint: Separate rows, before an overall view.

choices.text: Removing names from CVs
choices.why: That targets name-based bias at the screen.

choices.text: Scoring each rubric row separately, with its own evidence, before forming an overall view
choices.why: Right: separating the rows stops one strong impression spreading across all of them.

choices.text: Asking every candidate the same questions
choices.why: That targets confirmation.

choices.text: Scoring against the scale
choices.why: That targets contrast.

prompt: Put the steps of Renata’s debrief in order.
items: Start with the score that disagrees most
Ask for the evidence behind it
Ask whether others saw evidence on the same point
Decide, and record the reasons and any dissent

prompt: Why did Renata start Lucas’s debrief with Helena’s 2 rather than Yara’s 4?

choices.text: Helena is the most senior person in the room, so her opinion should be settled first
choices.why: Seniority is a reason to speak later, not first.

choices.text: Lowest, on a must
choices.why: Right: the room did not need to discuss what nobody doubted.

choices.text: Alphabetical order
choices.why: The order was chosen by where the disagreement was.

choices.text: To reject Lucas quickly
choices.why: Lucas got the offer.

prompt: Helena still disagreed when Renata decided to make Lucas an offer. What happened to her view?

choices.text: It went into the decision record
choices.why: Right: a recorded dissent is more honest than a unanimity reached by anchoring.

choices.text: Renata asked her to change her score to a 3 so the record matched the decision
choices.why: Scores may not be changed in the debrief, and the dissent was kept.

choices.text: It was dropped once the decision was made
choices.why: It was recorded, and fed the onboarding plan.

choices.text: It blocked the offer
choices.why: The rule needed a 3 on two musts and no 1; a 2 did not block.

prompt: In the calibration chart, for how many of the six candidates was Diego’s score higher than everybody else’s?
What did Diego find when he reread his write-ups after seeing the chart?

choices.text: His scores were accurate and the others were too harsh
choices.why: He agreed with the reading of the chart.

choices.text: The scale was badly written
choices.why: That is what calibration sessions find; Diego’s finding was about himself.

choices.text: He had interviewed the strongest candidates by chance, which explained his higher scores
choices.why: Across six candidates, the same pattern each time is not chance in his favour.

choices.text: He had been scoring how much he liked talking to the candidate
choices.why: Right: nobody can see their own leniency without the numbers beside everybody else’s.

prompt: A team’s debriefs always end in agreement within ten minutes, and the engineering director, who sits in on all of them, speaks first. What does this lesson suggest checking first?
hint: Fast agreement is not always good news.

choices.text: Nothing: quick agreement means a well-calibrated panel
choices.why: It may, or it may mean everybody moved to the first opinion.

choices.text: Whether the director has enough time
choices.why: His time is not what the lesson points at.

choices.text: Whether the debriefs should be longer, so that each interviewer gets at least fifteen minutes
choices.why: Length does not fix anchoring; order and written scores do.

choices.text: Whether the scores are written down before the debrief starts, and in what order people speak, starting with the director
choices.why: Right: quick unanimity behind the most senior voice is the shape of anchoring.
